h: Geese, poets and a historic airfield
p: House of Dun has a literary link too. The poet and novelist Violet Jacob was born into the Erskine family of Dun, and her writing about Angus life and landscape is much loved in Scotland. If you enjoy a good story, it's worth reading a few of her poems before or after your visit.
Allow two to three hours to do house, folk collection and grounds justice. The woodland paths make a pleasant loop, and if you've got binoculars, bring them.

That's because Montrose Basin is one of the great wildlife spectacles of eastern Scotland. In autumn, tens of thousands of pink-footed geese arrive to spend the winter, and seeing them fly in at dusk, honking overhead in long skeins, is unforgettable. Through the year there are waders, ducks and plenty more to keep birdwatchers busy.

Montrose has a surprising aviation story as well. The Montrose Air Station Heritage Centre tells the story of what's often described as Britain's first operational military airfield, set up in 1913, with aircraft, memorabilia and a strong sense of the people who served there.

Then there's the town itself: a wide high street, a long sandy beach backed by dunes and a lovely golf links. Head inland instead and Brechin has a fine cathedral with an ancient round tower beside it, one of only two of its kind on the Scottish mainland. Put a couple of these together and you've got a properly varied day out in Angus.
